ai.literal: Arrogance and, anger and, pettiness and, those who do not have, their prosperity, of a dignified, nature is.
ai.translation: The prosperity of those who are free from arrogance, anger, and pettiness possesses the quality of true dignity.
ai.modern: செருக்கு, கோபம், சிறுமைக்குணம் ஆகியவற்றை இல்லாதவர்களுடைய செல்வப் பெருக்கம் பெருமைக்குரிய தன்மையைக் கொண்டதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights three major flaws that can ruin a person's life: arrogance, anger, and pettiness of character. The author states that the wealth and prosperity of those who are completely free from these three vices possess a natural dignity and greatness. Without these flaws, one's success is respected and enduring, whereas prosperity accompanied by these vices is hollow and short-lived. Thus, avoiding these faults is essential for true, dignified greatness.

ai.literal: And stinginess, pride that has exceeded dignity, and improper joy, are faults to a ruler.
ai.translation: Stinginess, excessive pride that goes beyond dignity, and improper joy are ruinous faults in a leader.
ai.modern: கஞ்சத்தனமும், பெருந்தன்மை கடந்த வீண் பெருமிதமும், தகுதியற்ற மகிழ்ச்சியும் ஒரு தலைவனுக்குக் குற்றங்கள் ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet identifies three major flaws that can ruin a leader. First is 'ivaṟal' (stinginess), which prevents a ruler from being generous to those in need. Second is 'māṉam' (pride) that has exceeded 'māṇpu' (dignity), meaning an arrogant, excessive pride that goes beyond honorable self-respect. Third is 'māṇā uvakai' (improper joy), which refers to taking pleasure in unworthy, unethical, or trivial things. The poet warns that these three traits are 'ētam' (ruinous faults) for anyone in authority.

ai.literal: Even if a fault as small as a millet seed comes, those who fear disgrace will consider it as large as a palmyra palm.
ai.translation: Those who shrink from disgrace will regard a fault as huge as a palmyra palm, even if it is as tiny as a millet seed.
ai.modern: பழிக்கு அஞ்சுகின்றவர்கள், தினை அளவு சிறிய குற்றம் தமக்கு நேர்ந்தாலும், அதனைப் பனை மர அளவு பெரியதாகக் கருதி எச்சரிக்கையோடு இருப்பார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the extreme vigilance of noble people who dread disgrace. The poet contrasts two well-known objects of vastly different sizes: the tiny millet seed ('தினை') and the massive palmyra palm ('பனை'). Those who fear blame ('பழிநாணுவார்') do not ignore even the smallest slip-up; instead, they treat a minuscule error as a monumental disaster. By magnifying their own minor faults, they actively correct themselves and preserve their flawless character.

ai.literal: Guard against faults indeed as a matter of importance; fault indeed is the enemy that brings ruin.
ai.translation: Guard against faults as a matter of utmost importance; for one's own fault is the very enemy that brings ultimate ruin.
ai.modern: குற்றங்களை ஒரு முக்கியமான கடமையாகக் கருதி அவற்றிலிருந்து தம்மைக் காத்துக் கொள்ள வேண்டும்; ஏனெனில், குற்றமே ஒருவருக்கு அழிவைத் தரும் பகையாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the critical need to avoid personal faults and flaws. The author advises that guarding oneself against committing faults (kuṟṟam) should be treated as a matter of supreme importance (poruḷ). This is because a person's own flaws are not minor errors, but rather the very enemy (pakai) that brings about their ultimate ruin (aṟṟam). By personifying faults as a destructive enemy, the verse warns that self-destruction comes from within through one's own uncorrected mistakes.

ai.literal: Before danger comes, the life of one who does not guard himself will be destroyed like a stack of straw before fire.
ai.translation: The life of one who does not guard himself before danger arrives will be destroyed like a stack of straw before a fire.
ai.modern: துன்பம் வருவதற்கு முன்பே தன்னைத் தற்காத்துக் கொள்ளாதவனுடைய வாழ்க்கை, நெருப்பின் முன்னால் உள்ள வைக்கோல் போர் போல அழிந்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute necessity of foresight and preventive action. The word 'வருமுன்னர்' refers to the period before a mistake or danger actually manifests, while 'காவாதான்' describes a person who fails to guard themselves during this window. The poet uses a vivid simile, comparing such an unprepared person's life to a stack of straw ('வைத்தூறு') placed in front of a fire ('எரிமுன்னர்'). Just as dry straw is instantly and completely consumed by fire, the life of someone who does not anticipate and prevent faults will be swiftly ruined when adversity strikes.

words.gloss: if one is able to examine

ai.literal: One's own fault having removed, others' fault if able to examine, what fault will happen to the leader?
ai.translation: If a leader first removes their own faults and then examines the faults of others, what fault can ever come upon them?
ai.modern: தலைவன் தன் குற்றத்தை முதலில் நீக்கிவிட்டு, அதன் பிறகு பிறருடைய குற்றத்தை ஆராய்ந்து பார்ப்பானானால், அவனுக்கு என்ன குற்றம் நேரிடும்?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the essential quality of self-correction in leadership. A leader must first identify and eliminate their own flaws before attempting to judge or correct the mistakes of others. If a leader possesses this level of self-awareness and integrity, no blame or failure can ever touch them. The word 'iṟai' refers to a leader or ruler, and 'kāṇkiṟpin' emphasizes the capacity to examine or judge others' faults only after self-rectification.

ai.literal: The wealth of him who, without doing things that ought to be done, is miserly, without any way of surviving, will perish.
ai.translation: The wealth of a miserly person, who fails to perform the duties he ought to do, will surely perish without any chance of survival.
ai.modern: செய்ய வேண்டிய கடமைகளைச் செய்யாமல் கஞ்சத்தனமாக வாழ்பவனுடைய செல்வம், தப்பிப் பிழைக்கும் வழியின்றி அழிந்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the twin vices of neglecting one's duties and hoarding wealth out of miserliness. The word 'செயற்பால' refers to actions or duties that are fit and necessary to be performed, such as charity or civic duties. 'இவறியான்' describes a miser who hoards wealth instead of spending it on these necessary duties. The poet states that the wealth of such a person has no way of escaping ('உயற்பாலது அன்றி') and is destined to be completely ruined ('கெடும்').

ai.literal: The grasping mind called stinginess, among any faults, to be counted as one is not.
ai.translation: The grasping nature known as stinginess is a vice so low that it cannot even be counted among any other faults.
ai.modern: பற்றுள்ளம் என்று சொல்லப்படும் கஞ்சத்தனம், எந்தக் குற்றங்களுக்குள்ளும் சேர்த்து எண்ணத் தகுந்தது அன்று.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the severity of stinginess, referred to here as a grasping mind (patṟuḷḷam) or miserliness (ivaṟanmai). The author states that this vice is so base and destructive that it cannot even be classified or counted among regular faults (etṟuḷḷum eṇṇap paṭuvatu onṟu anṟu). While other faults might have some context or limit, absolute stinginess utterly degrades a person's character, placing it beyond the pale of ordinary human flaws. It is a unique and incomparable defect that ruins a person completely.

ai.literal: Do not admire at any time oneself; do not desire goodness-not-yielding action.
ai.translation: Never indulge in self-admiration, and never desire to perform actions that do not yield any good.
ai.modern: எக்காலத்திலும் தன்னைத்தானே வியந்து பாராட்டக் கூடாது; நன்மையைத் தராத செயல்களைச் செய்ய விரும்பக் கூடாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against two major self-destructive tendencies: vanity and unproductive action. The word 'வியவற்க' commands us not to praise or be conceited about ourselves, while 'எஞ்ஞான்றும்' emphasizes that this rule of humility applies at all times without exception. The second part uses 'நயவற்க' to warn against desiring or choosing to do 'நன்றி பயவா வினை', which refers to deeds that fail to produce any real benefit or goodness. Together, these instructions guide a person to remain humble and focus only on meaningful, ethical actions.

words.gloss: if one is able to manage

ai.literal: If [one] can manage [one's] desired things without [one's] desire being known, the schemes of enemies [will become] useless.
ai.translation: If a leader can indulge in their desires without letting others know of their attachment, the hostile schemes of their enemies will prove utterly useless.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் தமக்கு விருப்பமானவற்றை, தன் விருப்பம் பிறருக்குத் தெரியாதவாறு அனுபவிக்கவோ அல்லது நடத்தவோ முடியுமானால், அவருடைய பகைவர்களின் சதித் திட்டங்கள் யாவும் பயனற்றவை ஆகிவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains how a leader can protect themselves from the schemes of adversaries by concealing their personal desires. If enemies discover what a leader loves or craves, they will exploit that vulnerability to plot against them. However, if the leader can manage their desires in such a secret way that no one else knows about their attachment, then the enemies' strategic plots (நூல்) will fail and become completely ineffective (ஏதில). Thus, keeping one's personal desires hidden is a vital shield against external threats.
